<h3 id="scheduling-the-overlaps" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#scheduling-the-overlaps" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Scheduling the overlaps</h3>
<p>Once the communication granularity is decided, the next question is how to schedule the different tasks (dispatch, combine, FFN) on GPUs so that the overlap happens efficiently. To do this, we employ the inter-SM overlapping technique, in which we assign some SMs to the expert FFNs (comp SMs) and some to dispatch/combine (comms SMs), and have the two groups signal each other through a local counter. This is possible because with Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) loads and stores, we can fully saturate NVLink bandwidth with <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13940" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">less than a third of the SMs</a>.</p>
<p>We use inter-SM overlapping as our base strategy. In the MoE forward pass, the comms SMs begin the pull-based dispatch all-to-all and signal the comp SMs each time a full minibatch of tokens has arrived and is ready for computation. The comp SMs then run MLP-SwiGLU atomically on those tokens, and once everything through the down projection is complete, they signal the comms SMs that the tokens are ready for combine.</p>
<p>Comms SMs go through all of dispatch tasks before doing any combine all-to-all tasks, so many completion signals arrive from the comp SMs by the time comms SMs are done with dispatch. Comms SMs will then move on to the push-based combine while the comp SMs finish the FFNs for the last-arriving tokens. Additionally, we can fit in shared expert FFN while the comp SMs wait for the first dispatch to complete.</p>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="Minibatch-only MoK forward schedule" loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="media-light transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-light-rpB7k0EeXrBjPyO5DNDtH44ki6cPB5.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-light-rpB7k0EeXrBjPyO5DNDtH44ki6cPB5.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-light-rpB7k0EeXrBjPyO5DNDtH44ki6cPB5.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/><img alt="Minibatch-only MoK forward schedule" loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="media-dark transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-dark-Oy2SjizfH8J0QyfpdXzHQKP3169t1Q.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-dark-Oy2SjizfH8J0QyfpdXzHQKP3169t1Q.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-dark-Oy2SjizfH8J0QyfpdXzHQKP3169t1Q.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div></figure>
<p>The backward pass is similar, though it gets a bit more complex with forward replay (more on this in the next section). The comms SMs perform the reverse-combine and signal the comp SMs to run the FFN backward, excluding the wgrads (i.e., 3 expert-grouped GEMMs for 3 dgrads and the SwiGLU activation backward), and the comp SMs signal the comms SMs once the FFNs are complete and the tokens are ready for the reverse-dispatch.</p>
<p>We perform the three remaining wgrads after the dgrads for all minibatches are complete. We delay the wgrads for two reasons: (1) reverse-dispatch does not depend on them, so wgrads can overlap with the last reverse-dispatches; and (2) since the token axis is the reduction dimension for wgrads, accumulating over the full token axis at once minimizes numerical instability. As in the forward pass, we overlap the full shared expert backward with the first round of reverse-combine.</p>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="Minibatch-only MoK backward schedule" loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="media-light transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-2-light-7PsFKWZYeq5ckiMU3WfpOT00ZgsMfn.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-2-light-7PsFKWZYeq5ckiMU3WfpOT00ZgsMfn.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-2-light-7PsFKWZYeq5ckiMU3WfpOT00ZgsMfn.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/><img alt="Minibatch-only MoK backward schedule" loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="media-dark transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-2-dark-8TsLpdu0188op7l65z3vTQJIcCfrKZ.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-2-dark-8TsLpdu0188op7l65z3vTQJIcCfrKZ.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-2-dark-8TsLpdu0188op7l65z3vTQJIcCfrKZ.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div></figure>
<h2 id="fully-eliminating-cpu-gpu-synchronization-with-ring-token-buffers" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#fully-eliminating-cpu-gpu-synchronization-with-ring-token-buffers" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Fully eliminating CPU-GPU synchronization with ring token buffers</h2>
<p>The last missing piece is handling MoE dynamism; we do not know in advance how many tokens will arrive at a destination rank.</p>
<p>There are two existing ways to handle this. The first is token dropping, where any tokens beyond a fixed buffer size are simply ignored and never enter the expert FFNs. The second is CPU-GPU synchronization, where the per-rank token counts computed from the router results are sent to the CPU, and the CPU uses them to allocate exact-sized buffers.</p>
<p>Both have obvious downsides. We do not want to drop tokens for the sake of training quality, and CPU-GPU synchronization prevents the GPU stream from running ahead of the CPU thread.</p>
<p>CPU-GPU synchronization is especially costly on GB300 NVL72s because the integrated Grace CPUs are very slow. Our traces often show GPU kernels bottlenecked by CPU work such as logging or pushing training metrics to a remote server, even though the same training stack caused no such problems on DGX machines with Intel CPUs. Given this, we want to minimize CPU-GPU synchronization as much as possible.</p>
<p>In MoK, we resolve this with a ring token buffer, which we call <strong>macrobatch</strong>. Instead of allocating a large, mostly unused destination buffer for the comms SMs to transfer tokens into, we create a fixed-size ring buffer of a few hundred megabytes and cycle through it at minibatch granularity.</p>
<p>Implementing macrobatching efficiently requires careful overlap of computation and communication. Neither should stall because a buffer slot is still in use or because its data has not yet arrived. Ideally, we overlap across the ring boundary, computing on the tail end of the buffer while dispatching into its start.</p>
<p>The key idea is to drain each slot as early as performance allows so that it can be reused as early as possible. In the forward pass, dispatch fills slots and combine drains them, freeing them for the next dispatch.</p>
<p>However, if we run all dispatches followed by all combines (as in the previous section&#x27;s schedule), the next macrobatch cannot begin until every combine has finished, and computation and communication only start overlapping again after its first dispatch completes.</p>
<p>To avoid this, we perform dispatch-combine interleaving for the forward pass. The combine for a minibatch of the previous macrobatch is interleaved with the dispatch for the corresponding minibatch of the next macrobatch, which uses the same region of the ring buffer. This way, the buffer is refilled as soon as it is emptied. Note that the first macrobatch&#x27;s dispatches and the last macrobatch&#x27;s combines are not interleaved, as they do not have their counterparts.</p>
<figure><div class="media-border-container overflow-hidden"><img alt="MoK forward schedule at a macrobatch boundary" loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="media-light transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-3-light-6sCFZaei9WotkdFUDJewSnWO1BuMvG.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-3-light-6sCFZaei9WotkdFUDJewSnWO1BuMvG.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-3-light-6sCFZaei9WotkdFUDJewSnWO1BuMvG.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/><img alt="MoK forward schedule at a macrobatch boundary" loading="lazy" width="800" height="450" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="media-dark transition-opacity duration-[220ms] ease-[var(--ease-out-spring)] will-change-[opacity] opacity-0" style="color:transparent" srcSet="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-3-dark-tlhWhNcxFQX3Ohofubq8GmUBjX1595.png&amp;w=828&amp;q=70 1x, /marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-3-dark-tlhWhNcxFQX3Ohofubq8GmUBjX1595.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70 2x" src="/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fminibatch-3-dark-tlhWhNcxFQX3Ohofubq8GmUBjX1595.png&amp;w=1920&amp;q=70"/></div></figure>
<h3 id="reversed-ring-to-minimize-forward-replay-during-backward" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#reversed-ring-to-minimize-forward-replay-during-backward" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Reversed ring to minimize forward replay during backward</h3>
<p>The backward pass is slightly more complex because the backward megakernel must support forward activation replay. The macrobatch buffer is a ring, so if there are multiple macrobatches, some saved activations are overwritten during the forward pass and must be recomputed. The replay only needs to run up to the SwiGLU activation, since backward only needs the down projection&#x27;s input activation and output gradient, not its forward output.</p>
<p>One key optimization here is the reversed ring. If we consume tokens in ascending macrobatch order, the last macrobatch leaves the ring buffer partially filled, and the backward pass ends up with more activations to replay. MoK therefore walks through the tokens in reverse macrobatch order during the forward pass, so that the saved ring buffer is always either completely full or contains all of the tokens, minimizing forward replay during the backward pass.</p>
<h2 id="other-features-and-implementation-details" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#other-features-and-implementation-details" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Other features and implementation details</h2>
<h3 id="megakernel" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#megakernel" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Megakernel</h3>
<p>We built MoK using the <a href="https://hazyresearch.stanford.edu/blog/2025-05-27-no-bubbles" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">megakernel</a> technique, where instructions overlap at the SM task level instead of being separated by kernel launch boundaries. Megakernels are usually suited for fusing an entire forward or backward step, but we found the technique useful for MoK for two reasons: (1) implementing minibatching and macrobatching without megakernel fusion would require multiple kernel launches, increasing the launch boundary overhead; and (2) for inter-SM overlapping, we found multiple streams with green contexts unreliable at partitioning SMs exactly as intended, while software partitioning gives exact allocation guarantees.</p>
<h3 id="determinism" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#determinism" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Determinism</h3>
<p>For internal ablations and on-policy RL post-training, we designed MoK to be fully deterministic. The order of floating point operations is fixed, so the same input produces bitwise-identical output regardless of hardware scheduling and instruction issue order.</p>
<h3 id="cluster-launch-control-clc-for-rdma-overlap" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#cluster-launch-control-clc-for-rdma-overlap" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Cluster Launch Control (CLC) for RDMA overlap</h3>
<p>The MoK megakernel schedules its tasks through CLC to allow RDMA overlap. CLC is a hardware-native work-stealing feature introduced in Blackwell as a new way of implementing persistent grid kernels. A CLC-based kernel can naturally yield to kernels on a higher-priority stream without having to wait for the current kernel to fully complete. This matters because, during training, we often need to overlap intra-rack communication and computation with inter-rack InfiniBand/RoCE communication, such as FSDP all-gather, which require SMs of their own. Without CLC, the inter-rack communication would serialize behind the megakernel, causing significant performance degradation.</p>
<h3 id="mxfp8-support" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#mxfp8-support" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>MXFP8 support</h3>
<p>MoK supports both BF16 and MXFP8 precision modes. We train in MXFP8 mode, since it is faster and causes no numerical issues. In MXFP8 mode, the shared expert stays in BF16, as we found this to affect the training stability.</p>
<p>One added cost of MXFP8 is that tensors must be quantized before they are fed into the tensor cores. To minimize this overhead, we (1) provide an optimized MXFP8 quantization kernel for pre-quantizing the weights; and (2) fuse activation quantization into the dispatch all-to-all, the expert-grouped GEMMs, and the SwiGLU.</p>
<h3 id="router-weight-gradient-computation" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#router-weight-gradient-computation" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Router weight gradient computation</h3>
<p>The MoK backward pass also computes the router weight gradients, using a <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14080" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">SonicMoE</a>-style calculation. Instead of saving the full down-projection output, it computes them from the inner product of the SwiGLU activation and the down-projection dgrad. This computation is fused into the SwiGLU backward to avoid additional memory traffic.</p>
<h3 id="computationcommunication-sm-tuning" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#computationcommunication-sm-tuning" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Computation/Communication SM tuning</h3>
<p>The optimal ratio of comp to comms SMs depends on the workload. The local token count, the model shapes, and the hardware compute and network bandwidth all change how long the dispatch/combine tasks take relative to the expert FFN tasks. Even within the same workload, the optimal ratio differs between the forward and backward passes. MoK therefore exposes tunable parameters that set the number of comms SMs separately for forward and backward.</p>
<h2 id="speedups" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#speedups" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Speedups</h2>
<p>We evaluated MoK with two types of benchmarks: individual MoE layer benchmarks, for which we release all benchmark code, and end-to-end benchmarks on our internal production training stack across multiple NVL72 racks.</p>
<h3 id="moe-layer-benchmarks" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#moe-layer-benchmarks" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>MoE layer benchmarks</h3>
<p>We benchmark single MoE layer execution: global token scheduling, token dispatch all-to-all, expert FFNs, token combine all-to-all, and the final weighted sum. We benchmarked the forward and backward passes separately, in both BF16 and MXFP8 modes. All tests ran within a single NVL72 rack, with EP degree 64 and 2,048 tokens/GPU before routing.</p>
<p>We chose baselines that (1) support both the MoE forward and backward passes; and (2) run on NVL72s:</p>
<ul>
<li>NCCL + PyTorch</li>
<li>DeepEP + PyTorch</li>
<li>DeepEP + TransformerEngine</li>
<li>HybridEP + Megatron, which is Nvidia&#x27;s recommended option on NVL72s over DeepEP + Megatron</li>
</ul>
<p>We tested the shapes of widely used open-weight models:</p>
<ul>

<p>Overall, we observe that MoK is up to 2.37x faster for the MXFP8 forward, 1.78x for the MXFP8 backward, 1.92x for the BF16 forward, and 1.58x for the BF16 backward, compared to the fastest baseline.</p>
<h3 id="end-to-end-benchmarks" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#end-to-end-benchmarks" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>End-to-end benchmarks</h3>
<p>In addition to the benchmarks against publicly available implementations, we report speedups on our internal production training stack. Previously, our training stack relied on a DeepEP-based implementation with custom MXFP8 MoE computation kernels for expert-parallelism. We compare the end-to-end tokens per second metric by varying the MoE layer implementation choice (DeepEP vs MoK). The benchmarks were conducted on 512 GPUs across several GB300 NVL72 racks.</p>

<div class="table-wrapper"><table><thead><tr><th></th><th>DeepEP-based</th><th>MoK</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Tokens / second / GPU</td><td>760.9</td><td>1,070.2 (1.41x)</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p>Overall, MoK delivered an approximately 41% tokens-per-second speedup over our previous DeepEP-based production setup, allowing us to train our models more efficiently across our GB300 NVL72 infrastructure.</p>
<h2 id="megakernels-for-the-agent-era" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#megakernels-for-the-agent-era" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Megakernels for the agent era</h2>
<p>Mixture-of-Kittens is <a href="https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">fully open-sourced</a> as of today. We plan to keep maintaining it and welcome community feedback and contributions. Our hope is that this lowers the barrier to AI research, allowing more researchers and labs to train models efficiently. MoK also aims to be flexible. We put a lot of effort into making it easy to modify, so that with the help of agents, you can quickly adapt it to platforms beyond the ones we run on.</p>
<p>As a side note, with the arrival of AI models capable of writing performant kernels, the kernel optimization space has become a lot more interesting. Single-operator kernels that used to be written by hand are now almost entirely handled by AI. Given the right design directions (e.g., how to specialize warps, which PTX instructions to use), agents can one-shot state-of-the-art kernels.</p>
<p>Even more interesting, however, is the new capabilities this gives us. Last year, writing a megakernel required creating a layer of simplified abstractions like <a href="https://github.com/HazyResearch/Megakernels" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">this one</a>. This year, we did not need a framework. Instead, we removed the additional layer of abstraction and, with the help of agents, worked through the complexity ourselves from scratch.</p>
<p>Agents automated the simpler tasks (e.g., single-operator kernels) and helped us get through the harder ones (e.g., writing a distributed MoE megakernel) much faster and with a very small team.</p>
<p>That said, there is plenty of work ahead of us in optimizing high-stakes ML workloads that run across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. If you find this post and this type of work interesting, we would love to hear from you. Reach out to us at <a href="mailto:hiring@cursor.com" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">hiring@cursor.com</a>.</p>
